title: What Emotional Intelligence Actually Means When You Work in Tech
author: Colette Molteni
summary: Colette Molteni reframes emotional intelligence for technical professionals who bristle at icebreakers and team-building outings. Stripped of the fluff, she says, EQ is pattern recognition, hypothesis testing and feedback loops applied to the human layer of work, and emotions are signals in a system rather than noise to suppress. She walks through a daily standup in which a repeated "all good" may mask a shaky deployment, showing how to notice the pattern, hold a hypothesis as a guess rather than a verdict, and ask one specific question. She adds a Stoic habit of treating a first impression as an impression, not a verdict, and suggests using AI to rehearse how a hard question might land while insisting the pause itself is still the human's to hear. The article ends with an offer of coaching, but the framework is substantive.
points: Emotional intelligence can be taught to technical people as pattern recognition, hypothesis testing and feedback loops rather than as being nice.
Dismissing EQ makes technical brilliance fall flat because people ignore ideas that are presented in ways that sound arrogant or over their heads.
A repeated "all good" in standup should be compared against outcomes, and a pattern that does not match the results is a reason to ask one specific question.
Treat a first impression as an impression, not a verdict, and let it sit while you read the room before acting on it.
AI can summarize a standup or help rehearse a hard question, but hearing the half-second pause before an answer remains a human job.
quotes: Emotional intelligence, when stripped of the fluff, is pattern recognition, hypothesis testing, and feedback loops.
Emotional Intelligence, plainly, is the ability to perceive emotional data (yours and others’). You pick up on the signals. The words between the lines, so to speak.
As technical people, whether analysts, platform architects, software engineers…we respect signals. The inputs build our output.
The cost of dismissing emotional intelligence entirely is that our technical brilliance falls flat. People ignore it because of how we present it.
Notice your first impression as an impression, not a verdict. Let it sit. Get a pulse on the room before you act on it.
Deploying the feedback loop means checking your hypothesis and adjusting now or next time. That is emotional intelligence as a tech person, in action.
Your AI tools can summarize that standup in eight seconds. Clean bullets. Tidy action items. Every “all good” faithfully transcribed.
None of that requires you to be the most bubbly person in the room. It requires you to give people’s signals the same respect you give your logs. Not because it’s nice, but because it’s data.
